items.title: Mortgage market ‘still recovering’ from BoC’s COVID rate cuts, says lender president
items.description: The mortgage industry could be facing a much different environment if the central bank hadn’t decided to slash rates to record lows in 2020, says MIC executive
items.content: <p>The mortgage industry could be facing a much different environment if the central bank hadn’t decided to slash rates to record lows in 2020, says MIC executive</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639287200172090755.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The mortgage industry could be facing a much different environment if the central bank hadn’t decided to slash rates to record lows in 2020, says MIC executive
items.body:
The Bank of Canada is gearing up for what many pundits say could be the start of a new rate-hiking cycle – but the housing and mortgage markets are still dealing with the impact of its COVID-era rate policy even years later, according to the president of a prominent mortgage lender.

The central bank slashed its benchmark rate to a rock-bottom 0.25% at the onset of the pandemic, helping cause a homebuying frenzy as mortgage rates plunged and borrowers jumped into the market.

A series of rapid rate hikes in 2022 and 2023 put a halt to that housing boom, but Westboro Mortgage Investment Corporation president Derek Serra (pictured top) told Canadian Mortgage Professional he still sees the negative effects of the low-rate era seeping through.

“I think that we’re still kind of recovering from the decision to have lowered interest rates during COVID. And the outcome of that decision sparked such an incredible inflationary time for Canadians,” he said. “I’ve been in banking for 30 years, and I’ve always seen Canadians using the equity in their home as an opportunity for them to pay for their kids’ education.

“There was almost a kind of a familiarity or a consistency with expecting a little bit of growth in the value of your home. And so when these inflationary times came through COVID, which was triggered by the very low interest rates, the average Canadian saw rapid increases in their property values – which at the time sparked them to do more than what they usually do without, necessarily, the kind of long-term perspective.”

‘There was the opinion that rates… would stay low for a long time’

In 2025 and 2026, scores of mortgages originated during the pandemic have come up for renewal, almost always at much higher rates compared with five years prior.

That trend is part of the reason mortgage delinquencies are climbing, with Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) indicating on Tuesday it doesn’t expect the rise of mortgage arrears in Ontario to end until the middle of next year.

Serra suggested the Bank of Canada’s decision to dramatically cut rates in 2020 might have been the wrong one looking back.

“There was also kind of the opinion that rates would be low and stay low for a long time, and obviously that shifted for a variety of reasons,” he said. “And now we’re seeing the outcome of that decision.

“In hindsight, it’s always easy to look back and question, but you wonder if maybe we hadn’t dropped rates at the time, we would have felt more pain then – but it would have been a different kind of 2026 now.”

As the central bank embarked on a rate-hiking spree in 2022 and 2023, industry and expert opinion was divided on whether governor Tiff Macklem had misled Canadians by suggesting that interest rates wouldn’t be rising anytime soon.

Macklem told the House of Commons standing committee on finance in November 2020 that Canadians “can be confident that borrowing costs are going to remain very low for a very long time” – but within less than three years, the BoC’s benchmark rate had shot up by 475 basis points.

Critics said that reassurance may have convinced Canadians the time was right to purchase a home without factoring in higher costs down the line. Macklem’s defenders, on the other hand, pointed to unexpected developments including Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the further supply chain snarls caused by the emergence of the Omicron COVID variant.

Appraisal challenges continue in higher-rate environment

As well as causing challenges for borrowers at renewal time, the post-pandemic march toward higher rates poured cold water on a red-hot housing market. In that environment, appraisal challenges have arisen because there are so few transactions in many cities to judge whether or how far a property’s value may have fallen.

Serra, though, pointed to some recent cause for optimism on that front. “The good news is we’ve seen a little bit of increase in the past four weeks in purchase transactions, and that is a really good sign,” he said.

“It’s an early indicator… but as we see purchase transactions, even if they’re at lower values, we’re able to now properly assess where the market’s at. If you’re living in a community where there haven’t been any sales, it’s very difficult to substantiate the value of these properties, especially for clients who are looking for higher loan-to-values.”

items.title: GTA industrial rents fall in Q3
items.description: Outlook remains mixed for property valuations, CRE financing
items.content: <p>Outlook remains mixed for property valuations, CRE financing</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639287837545548261.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Outlook remains mixed for property valuations, CRE financing
items.body:
Industrial landlords in the Greater Toronto Area (GTA) are filling more space, but rents continue to fall, creating a mixed outlook for property valuations and commercial real estate financing.

Average asking net rents fell to $16.06 per square foot in the third quarter of 2026, down 4.8% from a year earlier, according to Avison Young's latest industrial market report. Meanwhile, vacancy declined to 2.6%, from 2.7% in the previous quarter and 3.2% a year earlier.

The gap between improving occupancy and falling rents matters for property owners seeking financing or refinancing, as stronger leasing does not necessarily mean higher rental income.

Despite the decline, GTA industrial rents remain 38% above levels recorded five years ago.

Demand for industrial space continued to grow, with net absorption reaching 2.2 million square feet during the quarter and 11.2 million square feet year to date. Logistics and distribution companies led leasing activity, with manufacturers, technology and pharmaceutical firms, consumer goods businesses, and retailers also contributing.

Major transactions included LG Electronics' 980,800-square-foot lease in King City, Brewers Retail's 679,400-square-foot lease in Milton and Amazon's 246,000-square-foot lease in Brampton.

However, leasing conditions varied across the GTA. The North recorded the lowest vacancy rate at 2.0% and the highest average asking net rent at $17.63 per square foot. In contrast, vacancy in the East remained elevated at 5.0%, despite a slight quarterly decline.

GTA Central was the only region where vacancy increased, rising 20 basis points to 2.4%, while GTA West recorded the largest improvement, with vacancy falling 30 basis points to 2.6%. These differences highlight the importance of local market conditions when assessing industrial property income and valuations.

Beyond location, property specifications are also influencing tenant demand. Industrial buildings with clear heights of at least 30 feet commanded average asking net rents of $16.84 per square foot, compared with $14.86 for buildings with clear heights of 18 to 21 feet. Avison Young linked this preference to businesses seeking more efficient facilities to meet changing supply-chain needs.

Industrial construction has also slowed across the GTA, reflecting broader Canadian industrial development trends.

Space under construction fell to 5.9 million square feet across 28 buildings at the end of September, down from 10.8 million square feet in the previous quarter. Active construction represented just 0.6% of the GTA's existing industrial inventory.

Another 48 million square feet remained in the pre-construction pipeline, but only 1% had been pre-leased. Avison Young said the limited tenant commitments suggest developers remain cautious about advancing projects without sufficient demand. Earlier reporting on Canada's industrial construction pipeline also examined the slowdown in development activity.

The 1.3 million square feet completed during the quarter had a combined vacancy rate of 12% upon delivery.

Meanwhile, industrial property sale prices moved in the opposite direction to rents, rising to an average of $378 per square foot from $355 in the previous quarter.

items.title: Equity shortages threaten Canadian CRE refinancing in 2027
items.description: Debt remains available, but lenders favour stronger borrowers
items.content: <p>Debt remains available, but lenders favour stronger borrowers</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639287835999782539.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Debt remains available, but lenders favour stronger borrowers
items.body:
Canada's commercial real estate market is recovering, but a shortage of borrower equity could complicate refinancing in 2027 despite readily available debt financing, according to the Emerging Trends in Real Estate 2027 report from PwC Canada and the Urban Land Institute (ULI).

Commercial real estate investment reached $16.2 billion in the second quarter of 2026, its highest level since early 2022, according to CBRE. Canadian investors' willingness to buy property has also reached its strongest level in 15 years.

Despite the recovery, lenders remain selective, favouring established borrowers and properties with stable income. With a wave of commercial mortgages due for refinancing in 2027, securing enough equity could be a bigger challenge for some borrowers than obtaining debt.

The report points to growing use of preferred equity and mezzanine debt to fill the gap between senior loans and borrowers' available capital. According to Lee-Anne Kovacs, national real estate leader at PwC Canada, these financing options could help property owners refinance existing debt or raise additional funds.

"Optimism is returning to Canadian real estate, but it must be earned. We are seeing clearer signs that the market is turning a corner, with opportunities emerging across asset classes and regions. The organizations best positioned for the next cycle will be those that remain selective, move with conviction and address the constraints standing between improving conditions and real opportunity,” Kovacs said.

The uneven recovery is particularly clear in Toronto, where the struggling condominium market contrasts with stronger demand for other commercial properties.

Greater Toronto Area pre-construction condominium sales fell 80% year over year in the second quarter of 2026, according to Urbanation, while completed, unsold developer inventory reached a record 5,001 units.

Meanwhile, CBRE reported downtown Toronto Class AAA office vacancy of just 2.6%, while Colliers placed the city's industrial vacancy rate at 2.2%, the lowest in Canada. These differences show why property type and rental income remain important considerations in financing decisions, even within the same city.

"The GTA's real estate market is moving at different speeds. Industrial and premium office show signs of recovery, while condominiums remain challenged. Purpose-built rental is supporting construction despite difficult project economics. Long-term investment opportunities remain, but realizing them requires patient capital and sustained housing delivery to prevent today's slowdown from creating future supply gaps and renewed pressure on housing affordability,” said Richard Joy, executive director at Urban Land Institute, Toronto.

Elsewhere, Calgary and Edmonton are attracting investor interest, supported by stronger economic growth forecasts. Calgary ranks first among Canadian markets to watch for 2027, with real GDP growth projected at 3.4%, according to Signal49. Edmonton is expected to grow by 3.0%, with continued interest in smaller industrial properties.

Across Canada, the report identifies senior housing, retail and industrial properties as the leading investment opportunities for 2027, although each comes with different risks.

Demand for senior housing is growing with Canada's ageing population. Cushman & Wakefield estimates that nearly 200,000 additional rental units will be needed over the next decade, although staffing and operating requirements add complexity.

Retail properties are benefiting from limited new supply and renewed tenant demand. Industrial investors, meanwhile, favour small- and mid-bay facilities, while larger properties face greater risk when they depend on a single major tenant.

items.title: Municipalities await future of housing law after change in B.C. government
items.description: The B.C. Conservatives have promised to return authority to local governments to determine where housing density will go.
items._ogDesc: The B.C. Conservatives have promised to return authority to local governments to determine where housing density will go.
items.body:
Local councils returning to work in the wake of the municipal election are waiting to see what a new B.C. Conservative government does with provincial housing legislation that forced them to redo their bylaws and official community plans.

During the campaign, the party promised to return authority to local governments to determine where housing density will go.

The promise was a step back from its threat a couple of years ago to repeal Bill 44, which was enacted by the NDP government in 2023 to stimulate housing starts.

The legislation required municipalities to amend their bylaws by mid 2024 to allow four to six units on single-family and duplex lots, effectively up-zoning most of the province.

It also outlawed public hearings for development projects that conform to official community plans.

The latter raised the ire of many residents, who felt they no longer had any say on what was being built around them.

Victoria Mayor Marianne Alto, who was re-elected for a second term, said the city is waiting to see if the next government has “profoundly different directives.”

She said the 2023 provincial changes fit well with the city’s existing approach to housing development.

“Frankly our own agendas were more assertive than that anyway,” she said, adding they also didn’t have any problem with the province setting housing targets.

“We knew we’d exceed them, which we have.”

The most recent data available shows the City of Victoria had issued 2,359 occupancy permits for new homes by late fall 2025, well ahead of the goal of 1,425. Victoria’s target is to issue 4,902 occupancy permits by 2028.

Alto said the city will continue on its current path, including policies geared at producing more affordable housing, until told otherwise.

She noted that the incoming provincial government has suggested it intends to push for more affordable housing. “I suspect that they’re probably going to look at ways to do that,” she said.

Across the border in Saanich, the Bill 44 changes and loss of public hearings were a big issue for many residents.

Outgoing Saanich Mayor Dean Murdock said revising the official community plan and zoning rules to accommodate what is called small-scale multi-unit housing — like townhouses and multi-plexes — was a lot of work for district staff.

Undoing it would also require a “significant” amount of work if that’s the direction the new provincial government chooses to go, he said.

The district also created policies to guide the application process around small-scale multi-unit housing, updating its building permit language. “Those things would all have to be revised,” he said.

“This could be a major diversion in terms of priorities that a future council may set.”

Murdock said new governments are typically “allergic to the policies of their predecessors,” so while they may recognize the value in creating more family-suitable housing, they’re likely to just rip apart the current legislation.

“The issues around housing availability and affordability are not going away, and they will be very much a pressure on a Conservative government, just as it has been for an NDP government,” he said.

The Conservatives have said they will remove red tape around housing construction, review the costs that slow it down, shorten approval times and overhaul the B.C. Energy Step Code, which sets energy-efficiency requirements for new buildings.

Mike Drummond, chief executive of the Urban Development Institute, the voice of the development industry, said blanket up-zoning had unintended consequences, such as making land assembly more difficult. “In the end, we believe municipalities should have more flexibility on where added density goes.”

Drummond is also keen to see the new government tackle some of the problems stalling projects, including building code changes and permanently removing the expansion of the PST to professional services such as architectural and engineering work. The proposed expansion, which was supposed to come into effect Oct. 1, was paused by the previous NDP government

Casey Edge, executive director of the Victoria Residential Builders Association, said he would like the provincial government to limit the cost charges that municipalities can set for developers. Such charges, which are collected for water, sanitary sewers, drainage, parks and transportation upgrades to service new development, add thousands to the cost of a home, Edge said.

Last term, Victoria council considered more than doubling the fees developers pay toward infrastructure needed to support new housing, including roads, water and sewer systems, drainage and parks.

Edge said the government should also look at replacing the Step Code, enforcing interpretation of its own building code and holding municipalities accountable for permit delays.

“There should be reasonable timelines for permits,” he said. “There is no reason a permit for a new single-family home takes two weeks in one municipality and months in another municipality.”

items.description:
Canada’s real estate correction has largely been concentrated in one province, but that may change soon. Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) data shows prices fell in September. The post Canadian Real Estate Correction Now Spreading To Other Provinces appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Canadian real estate prices fell in 8 of 9 provinces last month. Ontario and BC lead the 22.5% drop from peak, but the broader market is now sliding.
items.body:
Canada’s real estate correction has largely been concentrated in one province, but that may change soon. Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) data shows prices fell in September. All but one province moved lower, with BC going from resilient to leading the way lower in the past year. Other provinces, some of which hit record highs in 2026, are now making sharp moves lower. An anomaly or is the rest of the market ready to correct too?

Canadian Real Estate Prices Have Dropped $189k Since Peak

Before the provincial breakdown, let’s quickly review the national data. Canadian home prices fell 0.9% (-$5,700) to $651,400 in September, 3.4% (-$22,700) lower than last year and a whopping 22.5% (-$189,000) below peak. As previously noted, the lion’s share of that downward pressure is in Ontario—and to a lesser extent, BC. However, other provinces may be ready to join the correction.

Only One Province Saw Prices Climb, Nova Scotia Abruptly Plunges

Canadian real estate prices: Monthly change in dollars, September 2026.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

Home prices only climbed in 1 of CREA’s 9 provincial indexes. The PEI benchmark rose 1.4% (+$5.1k), but that follows a 4.0% (-$15.6k) drop in August. Bucking the trend and rolling back part of the largest drop in PEI’s history are two very different stories.

The remaining 8 of 9 CREA indexes showed declines. The largest monthly decline was in Nova Scotia (-2.7%; -$11.8k), driven by an abrupt plunge in Halifax. A 1.3% (-$4.9k) drop in Saskatchewan and Ontario’s 1.0% (-$7.6k), round out the three biggest drops lower last month.

Despite the broad declines, most provinces remain higher than last year. These gains are mostly concentrated in Eastern Canada, while the Prairies were stable. Newfoundland’s 5.5% (+$18.6k) climb puts it in the lead for annual growth. It was followed by Saskatchewan, which came in 2.8% (+$10.4k) higher than last year, and New Brunswick at 2.7% (+$9.1k).

Leading the way lower over the past year is BC, where September came in 4.7% (-$42.4k) lower than last year. Ontario followed with a 3.9% (-$29.6k) drop over the same period, followed by Nova Scotia, whose monthly plunge pushed prices 2.5% (-$11.0k) lower.

Canada’s Real Estate Correction Has Only Hit 2 Provinces So Far

Decline in home prices from peak, by province.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

Not one province remains at peak, though Newfoundland is only 1.0% (-$3.7k) below its July 2026 record high. Despite peaking in the same month, PEI has plunged more than double at 2.7% (-$10.5k). Neither province is that far from the peak, and all but two provinces remain close to the record highs.

Ontario is one of those two, plunging 26.7% (-$268.8k) since its March 2022 peak. BC is a distant second, down 16.7% (-$174.3k). That massive 10-point gap highlights just how concentrated this “crash” actually is. Nova Scotia sits in third at just 4.1% (-$18.2k) below its peak. But remember, BC’s decline was in the single-digits until well into last year. Nova Scotia’s abrupt monthly plunge could mean a broader correction is just getting started.

Whether Canada’s housing slump has another leg lower is anyone’s guess. The national index is down 22.5% from peak, but only Ontario has seen a drop larger than that. It’s being called a historic, 4-year market correction—yet most provinces are still hugging their record highs. Ultimately, corrections occur to resolve market inefficiencies for buyers, not just a national model. Until regional markets make sense to local buyers, activity will remain tame.

items.title: Millennium Ups Proposed Kitsilano Rental Tower To 26 Storeys, Adding Hotel
items.description:
Vancouver-based Millennium Development has submitted a new rezoning application for their project in the Kitsilano neighbourhood of Vancouver, according to a rezoning application published by the City of Vancouver last week.

The subject site of the project is 2158-2170 W 1st Avenue, two parcels that form an internal site between Yew Street and Arbutus Street on the southern side of W 1st Avenue, a few blocks south of Kitsilano Beach.

BC Assessment records show that 2158 W 1st Avenue transacted in January 2024 for $6,000,000, while 2170 W 1st Avenue transacted in August 2024 for $22,500,000. Each parcel is occupied by an old rental building, and BC Assessment values the parcels at $2,574,000 and $11,190,000 respectively, for a total assessed value of $13,764,000 — half of the 2024 sale price.

In 2024, Millennium Development — the developer behind Olympic Village — submitted a rezoning application for a 20-storey rental tower with 185 units and 20% of the floor area provided as below-market rental. The rezoning was approved in June 2025, but the project did not advance, and Millennium — through Millennium Kitsilano Nominee Ltd. — has now submitted a new rezoning application.

2158-2170 W 1st Avenue in Vancouver. (Chris Dikeakos Architects, Millennium Development)

The site was previously rezoned from RM-4 (Residential) to CD-1 (Comprehensive Development) as part of the previous rezoning application — enacted on June 2, 2026 — and Millennium is now seeking to amend the existing CD-1 zoning to allow for a 26-storey mixed-use rental and hotel tower with a maximum height of 301 feet and a density of 8.73 FSR — up from the previous 212 ft and 6.8 FSR.

The rental component will include 121 units with a suite mix of 33 studio units, 41 one-bedroom units, 31 two-bedroom units, and 16 three-bedroom units. Of the 121 units, 97 will be market rental and 24 will be below-market rental. The units have average sizes of 415 sq. ft, 512 sq. ft, 777 sq. ft, and 1,096 sq. ft for the market rental units, while the average sizes for the below-market units are all larger.

The market rental component will be at the top of the tower and above the hotel component, which will have 99 suites from Levels 6 to 16 — 9 suites per floor. A hotel operator/brand has not been identified.

Below the hotel component will then be amenity space, followed by some additional market rental units and all of the below-market units. The ground floor of the building will include the lobby, plus 6,294 sq. ft of retail space.

Millennium says in the rezoning application that “The project does not trade housing for hotel space” and that it "delivers secured market and below-market rental housing while simultaneously addressing the City's documented hotel shortage." From the proposal, 64 rental units have been cut, and the hotel component is being added along with six additional storeys.

The site falls within the Kitsilano North - Area B sub-area of the Broadway Plan, which allows for a maximum height of 20 storeys, but Millennium cited the Vancouver Official Development Plan (ODP) — approved earlier this year — and the Residential High-Rise 1 land use designation, which allows for up to 26 storeys.

“This application is being considered under the Broadway Plan,” said the City of Vancouver in a note published alongside the rezoning application. “The application requests consideration of height and density beyond existing policy provisions and proposes a hotel use that is not contemplated under current policy.”

The rezoning application notes that “The amenity program has been expanded beyond typical residential standards (greater than 10%) to provide a broader range of spaces that support wellness, recreation, social interaction, and flexible day-to-day use for all residents,” saying that “This modest increase enhances livability without increasing residential density.”

Renderings of the proposal for 2158-2170 W 1st Avenue in Vancouver. (Chris Dikeakos Architects, Millennium Development)

Another notable change in the proposal is the addition of a third elevator, which Millennium says “ensures that daily vertical circulation meets service reliability and accessibility standards in a mixed-use building of this scale.” To accommodate the change, the tower floorplate has been increased from 6,800 sq. ft to 6,923 sq. ft.

“The proposed 6,923 sq. ft. tower floorplate is a deliberate design response that supports the long-term functionality and performance of the building,” the application notes. “The modest increase in floorplate size accommodates a third elevator, significantly improving operational resilience, reducing resident wait times, enhancing vertical transportation, enabling more efficient structural grids, improving unit layouts, and creating a cleaner architectural expression.”

Although there are now no longer minimum parking requirements, the developer is proposing to include 164 vehicle parking spaces and 339 bicycle parking spaces in a five-level underground parkade.

After publishing the rezoning application last week, the City of Vancouver is holding the Q&A period for the proposal from Wednesday, November 18 to Tuesday, December 1.

items.title: Costly Construction, Decades Of Delays: Canada’s Project Leaders Get A New Playbook
items.description:
For much of the past two decades, Canada approached major projects with a simple idea: write the contract well enough, and the project would essentially look after itself. Each risk sat with a party ready to handle it, so when something went wrong, everyone knew who to turn to.

But it hasn’t worked out that way. Canada is one of the most expensive places in the world to build, and paying top dollar still doesn’t keep projects from running late (and over budget). That’s a problem at any time, but an even bigger one today, with the transportation, water, energy, natural resource, military and information technology projects currently being planned carrying multi-billion-dollar price tags — not to mention stakes in trade, sovereignty, national unity, and climate change. For developers and city-builders, these are the projects that determine where and how growth happens.

“What we’ve learned, in the last five to 10 years in particular, is that the contract is not going to save everything,” says Matti Siemiatycki, Professor of Geography and Planning, and Director of the University of Toronto’s Infrastructure Institute at the School of Cities. “We’ve realized that contracting is really a relational business, and that the relational skills amongst the parties who are delivering the projects are central to their success.”

The reliance on contracts has roots. In the early 2000s, public-private partnerships, or P3s, became the default for major projects, and by Siemiatycki’s account, most jurisdictions set up dedicated P3 agencies (many required the model outright). He assures that P3s do have their place. They just don’t suit every project, but the industry tried to apply them to nearly everything.

This history leaves many of today’s senior project leaders in a challenging position. They came up during the P3 era with “excellent project management skills,” Siemiatycki says, “but they were trained in a world that was very adversarial.”

The Canadian Infrastructure Leadership Academy was built to help those leaders move from contract-first thinking to the relationship-driven work major projects now demand. Launched by U of T’s Infrastructure Institute at the School of Cities and the Rotman School of Management, it’s the only executive program built specifically for major project leaders in Canada. It’s designed for public and private sector leaders with 10 to 15 years of experience who are preparing to take on the largest projects in their organizations.

These industry players already know how to run a project, so the curriculum builds on that experience, with a heavy focus on leading one: building teams when several organizations share a project, understanding infrastructure as a system, rather than a linear Gantt chart, and recognizing the biases that lead projects to underestimate costs and overestimate benefits. Negotiation and conflict resolution get dedicated focus as well, “because so many of these projects end up in some form of litigation or conflict,” Siemiatycki says. Rotman’s Geoffrey Leonardelli, Professor of Organizational Behavior and Human Resource Management, brings the school’s executive leadership expertise to the faculty.

Over six months, the hybrid program combines three three-day in-person modules at Rotman in Toronto with monthly live online sessions, mentorship, a capstone project, and the chance to work through a real issue from participants’ own professional contexts.

Graduates earn a certificate from the Rotman School of Management.

Applications are open now for the inaugural cohort, which launches April 13, 2027. Siemiatycki and his team are reviewing applications as they come in, with the goal of building an intentionally diverse cohort of leaders from civil infrastructure, energy, natural resources, and industrial projects.

The program’s model has a track record abroad; the United Kingdom and Australia both run similar academies. The Canadian version is distinct, though, in that it’s shaped to suit how projects actually get built here. “If you don’t understand our culture and you don’t understand how we collaborate, the projects ultimately end up in miscommunication, and things going wrong,” Siemiatycki says. “Having the program be by Canadians, for Canadians is really important.”

When that collaboration breaks down, the companies at the table feel it. “The risk is borne by the company, especially for construction,” Siemiatycki explains. “And if it goes badly, they’re going to wear it.”

Further, the academy puts public and private sector leaders in the same room on purpose. Over six months, each side learns how the other thinks about a project, and both leave with a network to call on, if and when something goes sideways.

“Ultimately we’ll build a cohort of people that can deliver for Canada,” Siemiatycki says.

The first cohort is where that network begins. Looking forward, the plan is to grow the academy into a national program delivered locally across the country, with each new cohort adding leaders who know how to work across the public and private sides of a project. Many of the organizations Siemiatycki has spoken with already see their participation as an investment in the sector, as well as in their own teams.

As that network grows, more of the country’s major projects can be led by people who already understand how their counterparts think, and who know who to call when things get difficult. It’s the relational side of delivery Siemiatycki says the contract was never going to cover on its own.

Applications for the inaugural cohort are open now, and organizations ready to add their people to that network can nominate a member of their team to apply. Applications submitted by November 30 receive 20% off tuition.

items.title: Sutton Group Announces Strategic Partnership With Ace Project Marketing
items.description:
Led by entrepreneur Ross McCredie, Vancouver-based Sutton Group has announced that they are partnering with Kelowna-based Ace Project Marketing, the latest move by the McCredie-led real estate company as it continues to expand its horizons.

The partnership will see Ace’s project marketing expertise and experience working with developers join forces with Sutton’s national network of over 6,000 agents in a way that the two say will benefit developers, real estate agents, and homebuyers.

As part of the partnership, Ace Project Marketing will be launching Ace Everywhere, a project marketing program designed exclusively for Sutton Group’s agents.

The firms said in a press release that the "program combines Ace’s centralized strategy, marketing and production capabilities with local agents’ market knowledge, relationships and licensed sales expertise.”

The result is Sutton agents will have support to work with presales, and Ace will bring its expertise to new markets across the country.

“For developers, the partnership brings together Ace’s insights into purchaser expectations and its sales and marketing expertise with Sutton’s national reach,” the companies said. “This collaboration offers a trusted sales and marketing pipeline, helping developers connect their projects with prospective buyers and the agents who advise them. By streamlining projects and maximizing presale success rates, the partnership supports market-driven developments and long-term success.”

“Combining Sutton’s national network of 6,000 agents with Ace’s customized market intelligence and project marketing expertise allows us to deliver data-driven solutions grounded in a people-first approach,” said Ace CEO Chad MacTavish. “Ace Everywhere gives us a practical way to grow alongside Sutton’s agents, combining the strength of a national platform with the local expertise every development needs. It reflects our confidence in the long-term opportunity for Canadian housing and our commitment to building the capabilities to support it.”

Sutton Group CEO Ross McCredie (left) and Ace Project Marketing CEO Chad MacTavish (right).

The Sutton Group team and Ace Project Marketing team.

“This partnership with Ace combines Sutton’s deep local roots across Canada with expertise in new housing, exactly when it’s needed most,” added Sutton Group President James Innis. “With new-home construction starts and preconstruction sales facing significant headwinds, we’re helping shape much-needed housing solutions that reflect the needs of each community, and giving our agents new ways to support buyers through a changing market.”

Sutton Group

Commenting on the partnership, Sutton Group CEO Ross McCredie called it “an exciting step forward in enhancing the services within Canadian real estate” and part of the company’s “technology-driven approach” towards delivering unparalleled value and homeowner-focused solutions for Canadians.

Sutton Group has taken several steps forward in recent years, after McCredie — through McCredie Investments — acquired the company in 2023. McCredie has spent the past few years positioning the company for long-term success in a technology-driven world and pushing the company towards a wealth-management model.

Those moves include the November 2025 acquisition of Ottawa-based real estate data technology company Homicity. With the acquisition, Homicity Co-Founder and CEO Jamie Blades joined Sutton Group as VP of Technology & Partner Success.

This spring, the company then announced a partnership with American luxury real estate brokerage Elliman (formerly known as Douglas Elliman) that would see the two companies create a new two-way referral program for their agents.

That same month, Sutton Group also announced that myAbode — an AI-driven deal processing “operating system” for residential brokerages — was making a strategic investment in Sutton Group and providing its brokerage optimization technology to Sutton’s agents.

Sutton Group has also continued to expand its footprint, opening new offices in Surrey, West Vancouver, Kelowna, Calgary, Stratford, and Gatineau-Ottawa over the past 12 months.

items.title: Bank of Canada Study Warns Rate Cuts Mostly Create Demand, Not Supply
items.description:
Canada’s real estate industry often argues the central bank should ignore shelter inflation and keep rates low to boost supply. A new Bank of Canada (BoC) staff paper tests both claims, and neither holds up as a blanket rule. The researchers find that ignoring shelter inflation during a demand-driven boom is destabilizing to the economy […]

The post Bank of Canada Study Warns Rate Cuts Mostly Create Demand, Not Supply appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: A Bank of Canada staff paper finds about 80% of the building boost from rate cuts comes from excess demand, and ignoring shelter inflation fuels booms.
items.body:
Canada’s real estate industry often argues the central bank should ignore shelter inflation and keep rates low to boost supply. A new Bank of Canada (BoC) staff paper tests both claims, and neither holds up as a blanket rule. The researchers find that ignoring shelter inflation during a demand-driven boom is destabilizing to the economy and pushes valuations higher. While rate cuts get more homes built, roughly 80% of that comes from excess demand created by monetary stimulus.

Housing FOMO Makes Ignoring Shelter Inflation Risky

Can the central bank safely ignore shelter inflation? Not when demand is driving it, according to the researchers. “Monetary policy should not look through shelter inflation when it is driven by housing demand shocks. Looking through creates a more volatile economy especially when faced with extrapolative expectations,” they explain.

Extrapolative expectations is a $10 term ($184.70 in 2026 dollars) for assuming a trend will continue. Home prices rise because that’s just what they do—so buyers who believe that load up on more housing and debt during a boom.

The researchers modelled a boom where home prices climb 20% over two years. Excluding shelter inflation from policy decisions pushes overvaluation as much as 2.2 percentage points higher than a policy that includes it. When buyers have rational expectations, the gap peaks around 1.3 points. In other words, trend-chasing led to a 70% larger overshoot.

“This amplifies financial stability risks, especially when price dynamics are partly driven by past increases in house prices,” warn the researchers.

Rate Cuts Are Steroids For Demand, Not A Supply Fix

Factoring shelter into rate decisions during a boom makes a hike more likely. Higher rates cool demand over time, but they immediately raise financing costs for homebuilders. Cheaper money means more building, argues the industry. In isolation, the math makes sense. Reality is a little more complicated.

“While financing costs do affect housing supply, supply-side cost effects remain quantitatively secondary to demand-driven mechanisms operating through house prices and expectations,” explain the researchers.

They modelled a 100 basis point (bp) rate cut, which lifts residential investment 6.2%. Cheaper financing accounted for just 1.4 points of that, roughly 20%. The other 80% injection comes from excess housing demand. Rate cuts technically get more homes built, but primarily by incentivizing more housing consumption.

Mortgage Interest Makes Rate Cuts Look Like Lower Inflation

After a rate cut, shelter inflation falls for about two years. That drop is mostly mechanical, as Canada includes mortgage interest costs (MIC) in CPI. Cheaper borrowing directly lowers measured shelter inflation, even though the real impact of monetary policy decisions isn’t fully reflected for 18 to 24 months. It’s a problem most countries avoid, including the United States.

Since CPI drives rate decisions and rates drive mortgage interest costs, mortgage interest creates a feedback loop. Rates fall, mortgage interest falls, measured inflation falls, and the BoC cuts rates to lift inflation back to target. The researchers call it a “policy amplification loop,” where easing reinforces the housing boom. It makes the case for ignoring mortgage interest, even as they warn against ignoring demand-driven shelter inflation.

We’ve covered this problem in depth before, so it’s nice to see it get some time in the monetary policy spotlight.

Hiking Rates Into A Supply Shock Slows Output, Not Inflation

When a supply crunch is driving shelter inflation, hiking rates barely makes a dent. Higher rates raise mortgage interest costs, offsetting much of the cooling in home prices.

Rents rise too. In the model, rental returns have to compete with what investors could earn on financial assets, so higher rates push rents up.

Responding to shelter with hikes “does little to reduce cumulative shelter inflation,” note the researchers. Total headline inflation ends up nearly identical whether the BoC reacts to shelter or not, according to the model. Economic output is a different story.

“In contrast, reacting to the housing supply shock leads to a significantly larger decline in output. This trade-off suggests that looking through housing supply shocks may be welfare-enhancing,” the researchers conclude.

Even the case for looking through shelter inflation comes with a caveat. They warn that if the supply shock persists, the risk of de-anchoring inflation expectations rises, urging caution.

What The Bank of Canada’s Model Misses About Rates & Productivity

The researchers are clear: the BoC can’t safely ignore shelter inflation when demand is driving it, and rate cuts aren’t a supply strategy. Hikes restrain home prices even in a shortage, but measured shelter inflation barely moves, since higher mortgage interest costs and rents offset the cooling.

What the model doesn’t show is the cost to the rest of the economy. The study shows a 100 bp rate cut lifts residential investment 6.2%, dwarfing the boost to output and business investment. In this scenario of a housing demand shock, residential investment growth significantly outpaces the boost to business investment and economic output. The model treats this as a passing problem: one shock, and everything returns to normal within five years. That’s not reality.

The BoC doesn’t cut rates once, then take a decade off. Repeated easing has pushed residential investment’s growth past the rest of the economy, concentrating capital in housing. The model has no way for business investment to lift future productivity, the exact problem that policymakers are currently struggling with. It can’t count what’s lost when that capital is diverted from other industries, nor does it measure whether, when or how it returns. The paper shows where the stimulus goes. It just doesn’t capture the full cost.

items._ogDesc: The Japanese retailer’s seventh B.C. location will join new Aritzia and Simons flagships in the former Nordstrom space
items.body:
Uniqlo will open its first downtown Vancouver store at CF Pacific Centre in spring 2027, marking the Japanese clothing retailer’s seventh location in B.C.

The Japanese retailer will join the new Aritzia and Simons flagships to take up the space formerly occupied by Nordstrom. The three stores are scheduled to open between 2027 and 2028.

“We are incredibly proud to support the growth of Uniqlo, Simons and Aritzia across Canada with these premier locations at CF Pacific Centre,” said Lillian Tummonds, senior vice-president of retail at Cadillac Fairview, which owns and operates the shopping centre, in a statement.

“This major transformation reflects our shared commitment to creating unparalleled retail destinations, and we look forward to the energy and excitement these powerhouse brands will bring to the heart of downtown Vancouver.”

Bruce Winder, a retail analyst, said the development is a "continued vote" in downtown Vancouver retail space.

"Downtown Vancouver has had a bit of a hard time getting tenants. Recently, it's been a bit of a tough sell for some brands to sign leases," Winder said.

"And they've had to deal with ... the exit of Nordstrom. Not specifically in [Pacific Centre], but Saks Fifth Avenue have left, going back, Sears left, etc. So it's been tough to fill these large boxes."

In November 2025, Vancouver-based fashion retailer Aritzia announced plans for a four-level, 40,000-square-foot flagship boutique at CF Pacific Centre, with an opening initially targeted for 2027. Cadillac Fairview's latest announcement tentatively puts the opening in 2028.

Earlier this year, Quebec-based retailer Simons announced plans to open its first downtown Vancouver store at the shopping centre. The approximately 92,000-square-foot location will span three floors and is scheduled to open in fall 2027.

Winder said several mid-sized brands have been taking up space previously occupied by a single large retailer in downtowns across Canada, including Vancouver.

Another trend he has observed in B.C. is the rise of Asian retailers as some American chains, including Target and Nordstrom, have exited Canada, alongside the closure of Saks Off Fifth stores.

"U.S. companies seem to have a harder track record, where some of the other retailers from Asia, like Uniqlo, Miniso, Muji, and some other ones, have done better in Canada," he said.

Uniqlo opened its first Canadian store at CF Toronto Eaton Centre in 2016, followed by its first B.C. location at Metropolis at Metrotown in Burnaby in 2017.

items.title: Bank of Canada now expected to hike key rate as it faces 'pivotal decision'
items.description: Expectations are rising that the Bank of Canada will indeed raise its benchmark interest rate this week as it considers the effect of higher energy prices on the economy.
items._ogDesc: Expectations are rising that the Bank of Canada will indeed raise its benchmark interest rate this week as it considers the effect of higher energy prices on the economy.
items.body:
Expectations are rising that the Bank of Canada will indeed raise its benchmark interest rate this week as it considers the effect of higher energy prices on the economy.

Financial market odds for a rate hike were just over 83 per cent as of Monday afternoon, according to LSEG Data & Analytics. The central bank's planned interest rate announcement on Wednesday will also include an updated monetary policy report.

The Bank of Canada has held its policy rate at 2.25 per cent for seven consecutive meetings.

RBC economists said in a note to clients Thursday that they are now expecting a quarter-point hike as the central bank faces a “pivotal decision amid evolving economic conditions.”

Last week, Statistics Canada reported the annual inflation rate rose to 3.1 per cent in September as the war in the Middle East continued to drive up gasoline prices. Excluding gasoline, the consumer price index rose 2.2 per cent year-over-year in September, easing from 2.4 per cent in August, suggesting higher energy prices haven't significantly spread throughout the economy yet.

Meanwhile, jobs data from StatCan released earlier this month showed the labour market stalled for a second month in a row in September as the economy lost 68,000 positions.

However, the RBC economists said they have “very low conviction” on a rate hike happening this week, and see a significant chance the Bank of Canada instead uses the meeting to set up a hike in December or January.

"While we don’t see an immediate need for the BoC to hike now, at the same time, a 25-basis-point increase in the overnight rate on Wednesday won’t materially change our medium-term economic outlook compared to a December or January hike," the note reads.

RBC assistant chief economist Nathan Janzen said in an interview that recent comments from Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem appeared to drive the change in expectations.

While speaking from the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok, Macklem warned that persistently high global energy prices will drive up the inflation outlook at home.

“That essentially just emphasized that the central bank is increasingly worried about the potential impact of higher oil prices on future, broader inflation pressures, and they feel confident enough the economic backdrop is going to gradually continue to improve,” Janzen said.

The Bank of Canada released its latest business outlook survey last week, which suggested that business sentiment improved on average in the third quarter. However, it found that concerns remained about rising costs and the war in the Middle East.

"All the economic data that we've had to date is consistent with the view that the central bank, the Bank of Canada, was getting closer to raising interest rates," Janzen said.

Canadian interest rates are still relatively low, he added, and the neutral range — where rates are neither helping nor hurting the economy — sits between 2.25 per cent and 3.25 per cent.

TD Bank economist Marc Ercolao said in an interview that it is clear the Bank of Canada is becoming more concerned about the persistence of rising energy prices, "and that's what's starting to change the calculus."

While a hike is likely, he said there are also arguments for the bank to hold its key rate.

"There's interest-sensitive parts of the economy, particularly housing, that are already dealing with higher bond yields and too much additional tightening risks some unnecessary weaker demand in that space," Ercolao said.

"Overall, Canada's economy is growing, but it's not necessarily overheating by any means."

The impact of U.S. trade tensions on overall investment and a weakening labour market also support a decision to hold interest rates, he said.

He said a hike on Wednesday would be a risk management measure to prevent the inflation shock from becoming more persistent.

Ercolao said higher energy prices are a double-edged sword for the domestic economy.

"On one hand, higher energy prices are good for producers and government, and corporate revenue intake. It creates higher incomes especially in commodity-producing provinces," he said.

"But at the same time, it's households especially that feel the pinch immediately from higher gasoline costs and then secondary to that, higher refined product costs end up feeding through the supply chain and into our end-user purchases."

Ercolao said that Canada has navigated the trade dispute "fairly well" by diversifying trade in certain sectors, including shipments of energy products to Asia and Europe.

"That said, there's still that acute pressure that's being placed on very reliant industries in Canada on the U.S., especially in Central Canada like Ontario and Quebec with our steel industry, our aluminum industry and our auto industry," he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press

items.title: District Energy Wants The Mechanical Room (And To Give Your Rooftop Back)
items.description:
Every residential tower gives up part of itself to equipment. From early plans, mechanical systems typically claim a room in the basement and a penthouse on the roof (the latter being prime real estate, mind you). This approach means that square footage is spoken for before the first suite is laid out.

Developers pay to build that space, but can’t sell or rent it. And today, with construction costs high and interest rate hikes back on the table, that cost is increasingly difficult to absorb.

“For developers building today, trying to make their projects pencil, taking capital off of traditional real estate development is a major factor,” said Diego Mandelbaum, Chief Development Officer at Corix, which builds and runs district energy systems as a utility across North America. “Reducing square footage for inefficient, building-scale mechanical space is a major piece of that, because doing so translates into both more usable area, and cost savings for developers.”

District energy moves thermal equipment out of individual buildings. In short: a central plant, usually located somewhere on, near, or below a project site, produces heat and chilled water for cooling and sends it through a network of pipes to every building connected to it, so the buildings themselves don’t need their own boilers. And because all of that energy is made in one place, the plant can switch to cleaner sources over time, like waste heat captured from a nearby power plant or wood waste that would otherwise go to landfill. This type of system has been around for well over a century — Corix’s district energy network at Ohio’s Cleveland Thermal dates back to 1894, for example — and now, the same central-plant model is helping today’s developers get space and capital back.

And those capital gains aren’t only about reclaimed square footage. Sometimes, they’re connected to meeting standards that are as well-meaning as they are costly. The starting point for the district energy system co-developed by Corix at Oakridge Park in Vancouver was a municipal low-carbon building policy. Meeting it tower by tower would have been an expensive effort — both in space and in capital. But that wasn’t the only way.

“At Oakridge Park, our solution was to rip out the mechanical equipment from each individual tower and centralize it. That allowed the development to meet the City’s green zoning requirements while saving a tremendous amount of capital and space,” Mandelbaum explained. At buildout, Oakridge Park will reach about 5 million square feet.

Oakridge Park (via Corix)

The savings can reach a project’s financing, too. CMHC is the only provider of mortgage loan insurance for multi-unit residential properties in Canada, and much of the country’s new rental housing is financed through it. And, CMHC-insured loans carry efficiency and sustainability requirements that are expensive to meet when approached one building at a time.

“We’re able to help developers meet these standards,” Mandelbaum says. In so many words, Corix can unlock financing solutions on a developer’s behalf, clearing a path to the CMHC-insured loans a project needs.

The earlier Corix is brought into a project, the more of those savings there are to find, since the team can help shape a master plan’s massing before plant spaces and penthouses get locked in. But no matter when the partnership is formed, the developer doesn’t carry the cost of the plant and pipes; Corix does, recovering that investment over the long term through the rates its customers pay for energy.

That means keeping those rates competitive comes first, and building too much, too soon would push them up. Which puts the pressure on timing.

“District energy doesn’t really work by just looking at an engineering study and asking, 'Can we make it work?' It’s about figuring out how to phase in your generation, and your capital, lock-in-step with the development," Mandelbaum said. "It's also about understanding that a developer will never give you certainty on how long it’ll take to build things out, because the market will never give you certainty."

So Corix builds in phases, leaning on modular construction and prefabrication to add capacity as buildings come online. At UniverCity, the residential community beside Simon Fraser University (SFU), work started with modular natural gas boilers while the community grew. Once the system had enough load, made possible by connecting SFU’s Burnaby campus, Corix invested in a much larger biomass plant, which burns wood waste otherwise bound for landfill. Today, the system heats the university and its neighbours, spanning nearly 5 million square feet in total.

Burnaby Mountain District Energy Utility near Simon Fraser University (via Corix)

Utah City, a sprawling master plan south of the border, is following the same path. There, Corix came into the picture after the first building was already up. Waiting on the grid wasn’t really an option: the development would have needed about 70 megawatts of power for its thermal systems, Mandelbaum explained, and the local utility would have needed 10 years to supply it.

Understandably, the developer had some questions about implementing district energy. But with construction in progress, the development team had tangible, tendered prices for mechanical equipment in hand, and could check Corix’s numbers against them directly. Spoiler: they held up.

“We built a modular plant in Washington state, we put it on a truck bed, we got it to site as soon as possible, and we got things energized within two years of the handshake,” Mandelbaum said.

Today, about 20 million square feet of real estate is set to be served by the system. Once enough of it is connected, Utah will see its own version of SFU’s switch: Corix will capture waste heat from a ~1.3-gigawatt gas-fired power plant about a mile away, which currently vents that heat into the atmosphere.

“What we're doing is closing the loop on what’s otherwise a wasted resource,” Mandelbaum explained.

Developments like these can take decades to build out, but Corix can handle a waiting game, thanks in large part to its ownership structure. The company is wholly owned by British Columbia Investment Management Corporation, which manages public pensions in British Columbia.

“We’re able to take a very long-term view," Mandelbaum said. "We have patient capital."

Utah City (via Corix)

That long view extends to everyone a system touches. Before a shovel goes in the ground, Corix looks at each project from every stakeholder’s side: the developer, the regulator, the municipality and, ultimately, the customer.

For Mandelbaum, the approach comes down to one question: “How’s a customer going to feel and experience this?”

And for the people who’ll call these communities home, the payoff lives in space reclaimed at the lower level, or on the sun-soaked rooftop.

“Just imagine," Mandelbaum said, "if every single rooftop was able to be used for amenity space. Or for recreation. Or for a garden."

items.title: Rising demand for multigenerational living reshapes B.C. home design
items.description: More than half of B.C. residents would consider multigenerational living, new RBC survey finds
items._ogDesc: More than half of B.C. residents would consider multigenerational living, new RBC survey finds
items.body:
More B.C. families are exploring multigenerational living to help younger generations enter the housing market amid affordability challenges, a trend that is influencing how homes are designed and built.

More than half (54 per cent) of British Columbians said they would consider living in a multigenerational home, the highest results among Canadian provinces, according to a Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) survey released earlier this month.

Among B.C. homeowners, 38 per cent said they would sell their home and buy one with their child to help them enter the market, also the highest regional result.

“In the last year and a half, I would definitely say that we have had an uptick at our company of inquiries,” said Suraj Jhuty, co-principal of Theorem Developments, a Vancouver-based multiplex and laneway house builder.

Many parents who own property in Vancouver and have adult children struggling to enter the housing market are now looking to redevelop their single-family homes into multiple units for family members to live in, he said.

The boutique firm is now working with four clients who plan to redevelop their single-family homes into four- to six-unit properties, with each family member occupying a unit.

“We are kind of getting out of this early adoption phase and a lot of families are seeing multiplexes come up in their areas,” Jhuty said.

Bryn Davidson, co-founder of Vancouver-based design and build company LaneFab, said his team has also seen growing demand for multigenerational homes in B.C., following the introduction of more flexible zoning requirements in some municipalities.

“First they allowed basement suites and then they allowed laneway houses and then they started allowing duplexes,” Davidson said.

“There are more options for people to build multigenerational housing on their own properties.”

The ability to create separately titled units, with their own financing arrangements and the flexibility to be sold independently, is appealing to families, he added.

“Laneway houses and multiplexes are spreading to other cities, you're starting to see broader interest in something that's been happening in Vancouver for a very long time,” Davidson said.

The trend extends beyond single-family properties, with some developers in Metro Vancouver incorporating multigenerational living into townhouse and condo designs through lock-off units.

These units within a townhouse or an apartment typically have separate entrances and full kitchen and bathroom facilities. One example is Juno, a condo development in Surrey that offers lock-off layouts.

“What I see in 2026 [is that] multigenerational living is not the same as the traditional model, where everyone eats at the same table every day,” said Inge Roecker, an associate professor at UBC’s School of Architecture and Landscape Architecture.

“It is more about creating shared spaces but everyone still has a totally private space.”

Benefits go beyond finances

Roecker said multigenerational living can do more than help families navigate affordability challenges in the region. It can also foster a more connected lifestyle that is common in many cultures and countries, and offer social and health benefits.

“Canada always says we are multicultural and then when I look at how we build, there is nothing multicultural,” Roecker said. “We traditionally build single-family homes and people are expected to fit into that family model.”

Families who want to live with their extended relatives, including those from South Asian countries where multigenerational households are more common, often have limited housing options. The same applies to single people who want to remain close to their families while maintaining their own living spaces, she said.

“We know now how much energy it takes to single something out, and the same goes for zoning…it’s a very unnatural thing and takes a lot of effort and energy to keep it up,” Roecker said.

“I totally welcome that we're finally looking at different models and how we create either your own family or families coming in all shapes and sizes in the 21st century.”

Multigenerational living can also allow young parents to go out occasionally without worrying about their children, as grandparents living next door can help with child care. Older adults may also benefit from having their children close by, according to Roecker.

About 73 per cent of Vancouver seniors aged 65 and over are homeowners, according to 2021 census data from Statistics Canada.

“We have no way to relocate all these people so we have to figure out [a way],” Roecker said.

In addition to laneway houses, duplexes and lock-off units, some developers are exploring housing complexes with shared courtyards where residents can gather and socialize, according to industry insiders.

“It's a newer phenomenon here in North America, but when you go to Europe, it is fairly recognizable,” said Jhuty, noting that his team is working on projects where multiple units share access to a courtyard.

Fragment House, a social housing proposal developed by students at UBC’s School of Architecture and Landscape Architecture, is an example of a design centred on shared spaces. The proposal includes a courtyard, a public café and a flexible studio for residents intended to foster social connections.

Roecker said the growing popularity of multigenerational living and higher residential density also require infrastructure and neighbourhood amenities to keep pace.

“We can have more stores, more cafés sprinkled in [neighbourhoods], we can have really nice bike paths and connect the [urban] fabric way better,” she said. “We can make the communities way more vibrant. … That’s my vision.”

items.body:
Time for your cheat sheet on this week’s top stories.

Canadian Real Estate

Canadian Real Estate Prices To Fall Even Further: Oxford Economics

The Canadian housing crash is already the largest on record, and it may not be over. Oxford Economics is forecasting prices and sales falling further through early 2027. Higher rates, elevated energy prices, and weak job growth threaten a recovery. The housing market is seen improving next year, though the firm warns the risk is still to the downside.

Canadian Mortgage Growth Slumps As Rate Hikes Threaten More Pressure

Canadian mortgage credit is slowly growing, and BMO warns it can slow further. Mortgage debt grew 0.3% in August, the second-slowest growth for the month on record. Annual growth was also the weakest since the early 2000s, excluding the recent correction. With roughly 30% of originations in Q2 2026 opting for variable rates, BMO cautions the Bank of Canada (BoC). Hiking too fast can hit a growing share of borrowers and throttle mortgage demand.

Canadian Real Estate Needs More Immigration, Foreign Buyers: National Bank

A whole generation of young adults want to buy a home but can’t afford it. They were pitched on the idea that more supply can fix that, but it turns out that’s not the case. Over 28% of completed new homes remain unsold, the highest level since the 90s. Unfortunately, prices are still out of reach for buyers, and National Bank says the show must go on. They’re urging policymakers to increase immigration and permit foreign buyers to boost demand.

Canada’s Borrowing 2.2x Deficit, Payments To Hit 1 in 7 Dollars of Revenue: PBO

Canada’s Parliamentary Budget Officer (PBO) warns the country’s debt demand is rising. Canada’s 5-year deficit is projected to hit $333 billion, but it needs $733 billion new borrowing—2.2x the deficit. It’s the result of a “growing stock of debt,” not rising interest rates, according to the PBO. Debt servicing is now the fastest-growing federal expense, with payments soon to consume 1 in 7 dollars of revenue.

Canadian Inflation Accelerates, Only 2 Provinces Below National CPI

Energy and shelter costs are helping to drive the Consumer Price Index (CPI) higher. Annual growth of CPI accelerated to 3.1% in September, surpassing the 3.0% upper bound used by the BoC. The headline is high, but just two provinces are lower than the national average. The rest are facing much higher CPI levels, especially in Atlantic Canada.

Toronto Real Estate

Toronto New Home Sales Rise, But Remain Weak As Price Declines Accelerate

Toronto’s new home sales climb but remain weak. September’s new home sales came in 63.9% higher than last year, but they remain 52% below the 10-year average. Most of those sales were single-family homes, where prices plunged 12.7% (-$180.8k) over the past four months. Condos haven’t fallen as much, but sales were the lowest for September on record. Even with taxpayers providing billions in incentives, the market is still struggling.

Halifax Real Estate

Halifax Real Estate Prices Just Made The Second-Biggest Drop On Record

The Halifax-Dartmouth real estate market may have finally run out of luck. The price of a typical home in the region plunged 3.9% (-$22.1k) in September, marking the second-biggest monthly drop on record. Sales came in 4% hgiher than last year, but they remain well below pre-pandemic volumes. The region has so far avoided the turmoil seen in Toronto and Vancouver, but last month’s sharp drop shows the region isn’t in the clear.

items.title: Northern B.C. housing market holds relatively steady as local economy recovers
items.description: The region’s home sales in the third quarter was 3.9 per cent below historical averages
items._ogDesc: The region’s home sales in the third quarter was 3.9 per cent below historical averages
items.body:
Northern B.C.’s housing market is holding relatively steady compared with other parts of the province, supported by a recovery in the local economy over the summer, according to the BC Northern Real Estate Board (BCNREB).

The board reported 1,009 seasonally adjusted residential sales in the third quarter of 2026, down 3.1 per cent from the same period last year and 3.9 per cent below historical averages.

The average sale price across the board’s region reached $464,180, up 0.1 per cent from the previous quarter.

“In comparison to other board regions in B.C., the North most closely follows its historical average sales levels, hovering between four to eight per cent below that benchmark across the past few quarters,” the BCNREB said in a release published earlier in October.

The board said the relative stability "has corresponded with a resurgence in the local economy over the summer, with our nowcast measure of Northern economic growth now closely following its provincial counterpart after a largely contractionary 2025.”

Much of this recovery is attributable to “robust” employment growth in the North Coast and Cariboo areas, according to the BCNREB.

Prince George recorded the most sales in the region in the first nine months of the year, with 1,043 properties worth $531.4 million changing hands, a 2.1 per cent decline from the same period last year. Fort St. John followed, with 541 properties worth $244.9 million sold, down 3.6 per cent year-over-year.

“The sales-to-active listings ratio remained largely flat from the previous quarter, hovering near 18.2 per cent, keeping Northern markets near the upper threshold of balanced conditions,” the board said.

Looking ahead, the BCNREB warned that inflationary pressures and rising bond yields have pushed five-year fixed mortgage rates above five per cent, potentially limiting housing demand.

Taking into account current national economic and labour market conditions, markets were also anticipating further Bank of Canada interest rate increases in 2027, according to the report.

“Despite these headwinds, we continue to expect sales activity in the North to outperform the rest of B.C., underpinned by relatively better affordability conditions,” said the board.

items._ogDesc: Halifax home prices posted their second-largest monthly dollar drop on record as September new listings hit a six-year high, despite rising sales.
items.body:
Greater Halifax real estate may be running out of luck. Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) data shows a six-year high for new listings in September. Sales also rose, but couldn’t prevent the second-largest monthly price drop on record.

Halifax Home Prices Post Second-Largest Monthly Drop On Record

The price of a typical home sold through the MLS across Halifax-Dartmouth.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

Greater Halifax home prices fell sharply last month. The price of a typical home dropped 3.9% (-$22.1k) to $541,700 in September, leaving prices 4.1% (-$23.4k) below last year. In dollar terms, it was the second-largest monthly drop on record, only beaten by the May 2022 plunge after rate hikes began. Prices are now 5.4% (-$31.0k) below the May 2026 record high, bringing them to their lowest level since December 2024.

Home Sales Rise But Remain Below Pre-Pandemic Volumes

Halifax-Dartmouth home sales through the MLS in September.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

Existing home sales rose but remain tepid. A total of 434 homes sold in September, up 4% from last year but still well below pre-pandemic levels. Rising sales aren’t an obvious driver of falling prices, but volumes remain weak—and look worse against elevated inventory.

Halifax New Listings Hit A Six-Year High For September

Halifax-Dartmouth new listings of homes for sale in September.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

September isn’t traditionally a big month for sellers, but last month was an exception. CREA reported 727 new listings in September, up 1.4% from last year. That increase looks modest next to sales growth, but new listings have climbed for four years straight. Last month saw the highest September volume since 2020.

Halifax-Dartmouth has largely resisted the price declines dragging down the national benchmark. However, that resilience was based on a relatively small pool of buyers. Thin sales leave prices vulnerable when those buyers pull back or when sellers face more competition. With listings rising and prices falling sharply, the market may now be testing where buyers are willing to step in.

items.title: B.C. billionaire's real estate firms allege 'pattern of misconduct' by CRA in tax row
items.description: Companies controlled by billionaire B.C. property developer Terry Hui allege that the Canada Revenue Agency has engaged in a "pattern of misconduct" in its attempts to collect on ballooning tax debts dating as far back as 2007.
items._ogDesc: Companies controlled by billionaire B.C. property developer Terry Hui allege that the Canada Revenue Agency has engaged in a "pattern of misconduct" in its attempts to collect on ballooning tax debts dating as far back as 2007.
items.body:
Companies controlled by billionaire B.C. property developer Terry Hui allege that the Canada Revenue Agency has engaged in a "pattern of misconduct" in its attempts to collect on ballooning tax debts dating as far back as 2007.

Five companies within Hui's real estate development group are targeted in the audit by the CRA, including Adex Securities, One West Holdings, a B.C. numbered company and two Luxembourg-based shell companies.

The companies filed an application in Federal Court this month, claiming the government has wrongfully moved to collect on tax debts totalling more than $200 million, most of which is accrued interest.

The application says the group is involved in capital-intensive real estate projects in Toronto, Vancouver and Calgary and the audit, initiated in 2013, focused on transactions that relied on Canada's tax treaty with Luxembourg.

The companies say in the application that they've received tax debt assessments this year, with Adex owing $45 million and interest of more than $65 million, while the two Luxembourg based companies owe together more than $92 million and $127 million in interest.

One of the companies' lawyers said in a statement that the total debt being sought by the CRA is approximately $219 million, due to "overlapping liabilities" between the entities.

The companies want the court to stop the government from collecting on the debts until a related case filed earlier this year is concluded, while objecting to the CRA wanting $115 million security payment from Adex.

Requiring a payment that large and not allowing the company to defer will cause the real estate group to "lose significant capital that is currently being used to fund active development projects."

The application is one of at least three filed in Federal Court this year related to the dispute, where they claim that being forced to pay will cause "irreparable harm" and that no advance notice from the CRA means that they "could not have reasonably planned for a debt … of this magnitude."

The companies claim the revenue agency has exhibited a "pattern of misconduct," alleging its officers acted outside established policies and procedures and "without regard to the impact of their actions on taxpayer businesses."

Lawyers for the companies were not immediately available for comment, but Justin Kutyan with KPMG Law in Toronto told The Canadian Press earlier this year that the transactions in the case were similar to a tax structure upheld by the Supreme Court of Canada in 2021.

The court ruled 6-3 in favour of Alta Energy Luxembourg, which had claimed a tax exemption on a capital gain of more than $380 million under Canada's treaty with Luxembourg, described in the decision as being "well known as an international tax haven."

The court found in Alta's favour, ruling that Canadian tax authorities couldn't use anti-tax avoidance rules to "judicially amend or renegotiate a treaty."

The dissenting justices in the case, however, said "the federal government did not deliberately set out to create the conditions for unlimited tax avoidance by means of schemes" used by the company.

The dissenters wrote that "the court should not legitimize such blatantly abusive tax avoidance based on the view that Canada should have negotiated different treaty terms."

The CRA said it did not have a spokesperson available for an interview to comment on tax treaty abuse.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

Darryl Greer, The Canadian Press
